claims.text: Equimolar FeCoCrNiMn high-entropy nanoalloys exhibit enhanced structural stability at high temperature.
Equimolar FeCoCrNiMn high-entropy nanoalloys exhibit enhanced chemical stability at high temperature.
The enhanced stability arises from formation of a stable, disordered solid-solution phase.
Configurational entropy of mixing governs formation or retention of the disordered solid-solution phase.
High configurational entropy of mixing reduces the alloy free energy.
The entropy-associated reduction in free energy enhances structural stability at high temperature.
The entropy-associated reduction in free energy enhances chemical stability at high temperature.
The initial FeCoCrNiMn nanoalloy is equimolar.
The initial FeCoCrNiMn nanoalloy has an FCC crystal structure.
The initial FeCoCrNiMn nanoalloy has an average grain size of 10 nm.
After exposure at 800°C for 10 hours, FeCoCrNiMn will show a 30% increase in structural stability, operationalized as a reduction in grain-growth rate relative to FeCoCrNi.
After exposure at 800°C for 10 hours, FeCoCrNiMn will show a 25% decrease in chemical instability, operationalized as a reduction in oxidation rate relative to FeCoCrNi.
FeCoCrNi is a conventional-alloy baseline that lacks the high-entropy effect present in equimolar FeCoCrNiMn.
The prediction is restricted to equimolar FCC FeCoCrNiMn with an average grain size of 10 nm exposed at 800°C for 10 hours.
Lattice distortion and grain-boundary effects may also influence stability.

contradictions.description: Oxidation rate is used as the measure of chemical instability even though testing is specified to occur in an inert-gas atmosphere; the hypothesis does not define the residual oxygen activity or another controlled oxidizing condition needed to make this comparison interpretable.
